title: An ancient civilization of millions once flourished in the Amazon
content:
conducted using airborne laser scanning reveals that a multicultural civilization flourishing in southwestern Amazonia between 600 BCE and 850 CE was home to millions of people. Spanning roughly 183,000 square kilometers, the Aquiry civilization built large centers for political and ritual purposes.

By surveying a representative section of the area, researchers identified the remains of more than 400 well-preserved sites of monumental ceremonial architecture, along with some later settlement sites.

Extrapolating their findings to the civilization's full territory, the researchers arrived at a cautious estimate of more than 20,000 ancient earthwork ceremonial centers. The largest known site covers 50 hectares.

Comprehensive surveys and radiocarbon dating showed that the Aquiry territory — which makes up less than 3 percent of Greater Amazonia — was already home to 1.25–3 million people at the start of the first millennium. This finding challenges earlier, more conservative estimates of the population across the wider Amazon region, which have ranged between 1 and 10 million. The Amazon's total population may have numbered in the tens of millions.

title: To Graze or Not to Graze? Finnish Dairy Farmers' Views on Pasture Access Vary Sharply
content:
As dairy farms in Finland shift to freestall barns, automatic milking systems, and larger herds, the once-standard practice of summer pasture grazing becomes increasingly rare.

Still, some producers continue to graze their cows while others have abandoned the practice. Both approaches have their own merits. Well-implemented grazing improves animal health and welfare while also enhances farmland  biodiversity and landscape values. Keeping cows indoors, on the other hand, makes production easier for large farms that may lack sufficient pastures near the barn.

When making Decisions about grazing farmers do not simply weigh grazing against other options in a neutral way, a new study based on in-depth interviews with 15 Finnish dairy producers reveals. Instead, producers tend to emphasize the animal welfare benefits that their own production type delivers best, while downplaying aspects it does not provide.

title: Luova Tuho – Johan Eichhornin valokuvasarja
content:
Johan Eichhorn’s Creative Destruction shifts human interventions in nature into the human living environment. Instead of forest roads cutting through woodlands, drainage drying out wetlands, and dams altering waterways, these elements appear in people’s homes and other everyday spaces. 

In the staged photographs, familiar environments become strange. At the same time, they make visible the ways we reshape nature – changes that have gradually become an almost unnoticed part of our daily lives. 

The exhibition does not aim to provide answers, but invites viewers to reflect on why we accept in nature things we would never accept in our own living environment.

Johan Eichhorn is a Finnish-German photographer and theatre director. His work has been exhibited in museums, galleries, and theatres in Finland and internationally. In his photographic art, he examines societal phenomena through staged and narrative imagery.

Research groups, artists, photographers, writers, nature enthusiasts, and others interested in nature are welcome to propose exhibitions for the Natural History Museum and the botanical gardens in Kaisaniemi and Kumpula.

title: A Semester with WORK-IT: Reflections from our assistants
content:
Q: What made you interested in joining the project?

- What drove me to this project was the combination of learning about history and science communication. Just before applying for this position, I became a board member for an organisation that teaches science communication for researchers and students, and being able to apply the information I’ve learned there straight to my work with WORK-IT felt like a perfect opportunity.

- As a student in the history disciplines myself, the scope of the project really interested me. I had already worked with event organizing with my faculty as well, so I also felt like I could contribute with my already-there skillset.

Q: What have been your main tasks in the team?

- During the spring, I was focusing on transcribing meetings as well as the workshop we held in March. We are also in charge of communications, so revising our strategy with the team and working with them on publications has been big. I've also helped one of our researchers with data annotation.

title: Three Decades at the Aleksanteri Institute, Hegel, and Soviet Philosophy: Interview with Professor Emeritus Vesa Oittinen
content:
Emyleigh Simoes sits down with Professor Emeritus Vesa Oittinen to discuss his career at the Aleksanteri Institute, his forthcoming book project, and his contributions to Russian and Soviet intellectual history as a discipline.

Since joining the Institute shortly after its founding in 1996, Professor Oittinen has helped shape its research agenda while pursuing influential work on Russian modernization, German idealism, and Soviet philosophy. In this interview, he reflects on the institute's early years in the aftermath of the Soviet Union's collapse, discusses his forthcoming German-language book Hegels Dialektik der Moderne (Hegel's Dialectic of Modernity), and explains why Soviet philosophy—particularly the work of thinkers such as Lev Vygotsky and Evald Ilyenkov—deserves renewed scholarly attention. The interview provides a fascinating glimpse into Professor Oittinen’s pioneering role at Aleksanteri and the enduring relevance of studying Russian and Soviet intellectual history. 

The conversation below has been edited for length and clarity.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Arkadiankadun siltaremontti aiheuttaa muutoksia liikennejärjestelyihin Luonnontieteellisen museon lähistöllä
content:
The renovation will start with the construction of temporary traffic arrangements from Wednesday 7 January onwards. The renovation is expected to be completed in late 2026.

A temporary bridge for pedestrians will be built on the east side of Arkadiankatu over the Baana. The aim is to maintain the pedestrian route on the east side of the bridge until the temporary bridge is operational. Cyclists will also be able to use the bridge.

The Baana route underneath the bridge is expected to remain open for most of the renovation's duration, with some minor exceptions.

There will be changes to the motor vehicle routes by the bridge and around it in January. If possible, should be favoured during the bridge renovation.

Connections to the bus terminals in Kamppi will remain available, but there will be a slight diversion of routes.

Trams 1 and 1T will run via Simonkatu and Kamppi. Lasipalatsi and the Natural History Museum will not be served.

The diversion is due to the renovation of the Arkadiankatu bridge and will remain in place until late 2026. The renovation will not affect HSL's bus services.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.

title: Tero Pajukallion valokuvanäyttelyssä tutkitaan suon värejä
content:
Tero Pajukallio is a freelance photographer based in Helsinki. His work consists mainly of journalistic photography and the photography of various events. Nature photography became an important part of his work in the 2020s. In nature photography, he is particularly fascinated by mires, forests, and landscapes.

– For this exhibition, I have selected especially photographs of mires because of the incredible colors they contain. When walking along boardwalks, the rich color palette of the mires is not apparent, but a drone reveals the full spectrum of colors. The images have been enhanced in terms of color saturation, so they should be regarded more as photographic art than as documentary photographs.

Colours is on display at the Natural History Museum café from August 18 to October 11, 2026.

The café follows the museum's opening hours and opens half an hour after the museum itself. Admission to the café is free.

Research groups, artists, photographers, writers, nature enthusiasts, and others interested in nature are welcome to propose exhibitions for the Natural History Museum and the botanical gardens in Kaisaniemi and Kumpula.
